content.question_text: Can you create your own custom exceptions in Java?
What class do all exceptions ultimately derive from?
How does the exception hierarchy first split, directly below Throwable?
Describe what the Error hierarchy represents, and whether you should typically throw Error exceptions yourself.

core_requirements: Describes internal errors and resource exhaustion situations inside the Java runtime system
Should not be thrown by your own code, unless deliberately terminating the program gracefully

content.question_text: How does the Exception branch of the hierarchy split into two categories, and what are those two categories officially called?

core_requirements: Splits into RuntimeException (unchecked) and all other exceptions (checked, commonly exemplified by IOException)
acceptable_variations: Answer may use 'RuntimeExceptions and IOExceptions' informally, as long as the checked/unchecked distinction is also understood

content.question_text: What causes a RuntimeException to occur?

core_requirements: It happens when you (the programmer) make a programming error

content.question_text: What do the non-RuntimeException (checked) exceptions generally describe?

core_requirements: Any exception that is not a RuntimeException — problems that can occur even without a programming error, often involving external conditions

acceptable_variations: Any 3 valid RuntimeException examples matching these categories

core_requirements: Reading past the end of a file
Opening a file that does not exist
acceptable_variations: Any valid checked-exception examples matching these categories

content.question_text: What is the general rule of thumb regarding whose fault a RuntimeException is?

core_requirements: If it's a RuntimeException, it's your (the programmer's) fault
Any exception other than a RuntimeException or an Error
